why: The CIAAW abridged table (ciaaw.org/abridged-atomic-weights.htm) lists Zr as 91.222 ± 0.003 and says Gd, Lu and Zr were revised in 2024. The field is defined as the IUPAC abridged standard atomic weight, and 91.224 is the superseded pre-2024 value at the same precision, so this is an update to the defining authority, not a style change. The numeric difference is tiny, and some older sources still print 91.224.

219 comes from PubChem's AtomicRadius column, which cites no source. Bondi and Mantina give no Y value. WebElements gives Y 275 pm and names Alvarez, Dalton Trans. 2013, 42, 8617 as its reference. Wikipedia's atomic radii data page lists no vdW value for Y. Under the stated Bondi/Alvarez convention, 219 is about 20% low, beyond the 10% threshold. 275 is the Alvarez value.

186 comes from PubChem's AtomicRadius column, which cites no source. Bondi and Mantina give no Zr value. WebElements, citing Alvarez 2013, gives 252 pm. Even Batsanov's crystallographic radius (about 230 pm, via KnowledgeDoor) is about 24% above 186. Under the Bondi/Alvarez convention, 186 is about 26% low, so it should be flagged. 252 is the Alvarez value.

Wikipedia's isotopes of krypton article lists 78Kr as a primordial radionuclide with half-life 9.2(+5.5-2.6)x10^21 y by double electron capture to 78Se (Gavrilyuk 2013 indication, Ratkevich 2017 measurement). It says natural krypton is five stable isotopes plus slightly radioactive 78Kr. The field definition puts long-lived naturally occurring radioactive isotopes under radioactive, as the dataset already does for Ge-76, Se-82 and Zr-96. So 78Kr does not belong in stable. The remaining five abundances are unchanged.

current: [{"A":85,"halfLife":"10.7 years","note":"Released by nuclear fuel reprocessing."},{"A":81,"halfLife":"229,000 years","note":"Used to date old groundwater and ice."}]
corrected: [{"A":78,"halfLife":"9.2×10^21 years","note":"0.355% of natural krypton; decays by rare double electron capture."},{"A":85,"halfLife":"10.7 years","note":"Released by nuclear fuel reprocessing."},{"A":81,"halfLife":"229,000 years","note":"Used to date old groundwater and ice."}]
why: This is the companion to removing 78Kr from the stable list. Wikipedia (from NUBASE) gives 9.2x10^21 y, decaying by double electron capture to 78Se. The note's 0.355% matches the abundance the dataset already uses. Putting the primordial isotope first follows the order used for Ge, Se, Zr and Rb, and the half-life format matches Ge-76's "1.8×10^21 years".

Wikipedia's electron affinity data page gives In = 0.38392(6) eV, from Walter et al., Phys. Rev. A 82, 032507 (2010), measured by infrared photodetachment threshold spectroscopy. 0.3 eV is an old estimate and is about 22% too low.
Vandevraye, Drag and Blondel, J. Phys. B 46, 125002 (2013), measured 1.112070(2) eV by photodetachment microscopy (Wikipedia data page). 1.2 is about 8% too high, which is beyond tolerance.

A precision measurement (arXiv:1712.03628, 'Half-lives of 101Rh and 108Agm') gives 4.07 +/- 0.05 y. NUBASE2020 uses it, and so does Wikipedia's Isotopes of rhodium (4.07(5) y). The old 3.3(3) y value is superseded and about 19% low. It also wrongly makes 101Rh shorter-lived than 102mRh (3.742 y).

NIST ASD, checked directly, gives Tc I IE = 7.11938(3) eV, from Mattolat et al., Phys. Rev. A 81, 052513 (2010). Wikipedia's molar ionization energies table gives 686.9 kJ/mol, which is 7.119 eV. 7.28 is the 1950s value, now superseded by a precise measurement, and is 2.3% high, beyond the 2% tolerance. The other IEs in this file match NIST, so NIST is the consistent basis here.

current: "Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other element and reflects visible light best of all metals. Silver ions kill bacteria."
corrected: "Silver conducts electricity better than any other element and heat better than any other metal, and it reflects visible light best of all metals. Silver ions kill bacteria."
why: Silver's thermal conductivity, about 429 W/(m K), is the highest among metals. Diamond (carbon) reaches about 2000-2200 W/(m K), so 'heat better than any other element' is false. Silver does have the highest electrical conductivity of any element, and the rest of the sentence holds. The proposed rewording is accurate.

German Wikipedia's lead gives 'Hieronymus Theodor Richter'. English Wikipedia's article is titled 'Hieronymus Theodor Richter', and 'Hieronymous' only redirects to it. Indium Corporation and the UNT 'Rediscovery of the Elements' pages also use Hieronymus. 'Hieronymous' is a common English misspelling of his name.

current: Bending an indium bar makes a high-pitched 'cry' as its crystals slip.
corrected: "Bending an indium bar makes a high-pitched 'cry' as its crystals suddenly twin."
why: Wikipedia's Indium article says the cry is 'a crackling sound due to crystal twinning', the same mechanism as tin cry. 'Slip' is the technical name for a different, quiet deformation mechanism (dislocation glide), so the current wording names the wrong mechanism. The corrected wording is accurate.

current: Named columbium; confused with tantalum until Heinrich Rose separated them in 1844.
corrected: "Named columbium; confused with tantalum until Heinrich Rose showed in 1844 that it was a different element."
why: RSC says Rose showed in 1844 that columbite contained both niobium and tantalum, and that the two are difficult to separate. Wikipedia's Niobium article says Rose determined that tantalum ores contain a second element. It credits Blomstrand, Sainte-Claire Deville and Marignac (1864-1866) with conclusively distinguishing them, and Marignac's 1866 work showed there were only two elements. Saying Rose 'separated them' is therefore misleading. The proposed wording matches the sources, and 1844 agrees with RSC and the Wikipedia infobox.

Barium has a well-established measured electron affinity of 0.14462(6) eV (laser photodetachment, Petrunin et al. 1995, Phys. Rev. Lett. 75, 1911). Wikipedia's electron affinity data page lists it with no caveat. Leaving it null omits a well-known value.

latticeConstantPm = 431 is the hexagonal-setting a of A7 antimony (Wikipedia: a_h = 430.84 pm, c_h = 1127.36 pm at 20 °C; WebElements 430.7/1127.3 pm). The rhombohedral primitive a would be 450.7 pm, so the matching hexagonal c is a well-known value missing here. lattice ('rhombohedral') differs from renderAs ('simple-cubic'), so the renderer does not use cPm, and adding it does not affect the drawing.
